1002.title: Who is hearing?
1002.hook: Bassui: ask who is it that hears?
1002.howItsDone: In some Rinzai Zen communities, teachers give students a single question such as Bassui's to carry through sitting and daily work, and check their understanding in private meetings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ikkyu, Crazy Cloud, who laughed at robes and ranks. Your line: the wild monk.

Right now there's a sound near you. A fridge humming. Traffic. A bird. A moment ago you didn't notice it; now you do. Put a strange question next to that sound. Not what is it, but who is it that's hearing it? It sounds like a riddle for a sleepy afternoon. A Japanese Zen teacher named Bassui made it central to his teaching, and told students to keep asking until the question itself broke open.
screen: `A SOUND, RIGHT NOW.` → `NOT WHAT IS IT.` → `WHO IS HEARING IT?`

segments.voice: Bassui was a Rinzai Zen teacher in Japan who wrote letters and talks for monks, nuns and lay people, and again and again he gave them one question: when you hear a sound, who is hearing? First, why hearing? Sound is always arriving, so the question is always there. No temple or cushion needed, just ears. Second, what the question is not. Bassui doesn't want an answer like my ears, or my brain, or me. Those are labels. He tells students to turn the attention back from the sound toward the one who hears, and look. They find no object to grab: no shape, no color, nothing to point at. And yet the hearing is plainly happening. Third, the push. When you can't find the hearer, don't give up and don't settle for a clever explanation. Keep asking, more deeply, with your whole body, the way you'd keep searching for something precious you'd lost. He describes the questioning growing until it fills everything, and then, at last, breaking open. Fourth, what it opens onto: your own mind, which he calls the true master, the Buddha nature that was never born and never dies. It isn't far away or reserved for monks, Bassui insists. It's the one listening to this sentence. Zen teachers use questions in different ways; some give a koan, some ask students simply to sit. Bassui's way was this one plain question, carried everywhere.
screen: `BASSUI: ONE QUESTION.` · `WHY HEARING? SOUND IS ALWAYS HERE.` · `LOOK FOR THE HEARER. FIND NO SHAPE.` · `KEEP ASKING, WITH YOUR WHOLE BODY.` · then, large: `WHO IS HEARING?`

segments.voice: Sit still and let sounds come to you, near, far, loud, soft, without naming them. Then gently ask inside, who is hearing this, and instead of answering with a word, turn the attention back toward wherever the hearing is happening. If you find nothing to hold, stay with the not-finding, and when the mind drifts, let the next sound call you back.
Bassui. The Zen teacher who told students, when a sound comes, to turn from it and ask who is hearing, and keep looking. Today's word.
Your line: stay with the not-finding. Every sound can bring the question back. Day one thousand two.

1003.title: The unborn
1003.hook: Bankei taught ordinary people: you already have the unborn Buddha-mind
1003.howItsDone: Zen students and teachers read Bankei's recorded talks and point to the unborn mind in everyday life; his way is often taught without koans, as trusting the mind that is already working.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bassui's question: when a sound comes, who is hearing? Your line: stay with the not-finding.

A man comes to a Zen teacher with a confession. I was born with a short temper, he says. It's just how I am. How do I fix it? The teacher looks interested. That's remarkable, he says. Show it to me. The man says he can't, not right now; it only comes out when something sets it off. Then, says the teacher, it isn't something you were born with. You make it, on the spot. The teacher was Bankei, and he told plain stories like this to ordinary people.
screen: `I WAS BORN THIS WAY.` → `SHOW IT TO ME.` → `YOU MAKE IT ON THE SPOT.`

segments.voice: Bankei was a Japanese Rinzai Zen teacher whose teaching fits in a sentence: everyone already has the Buddha-mind, and it is unborn. First, unborn. Bankei means a mind never produced, never put together, so it can never fall apart. It's here before you start building moods and grudges and stories, and it handles everything perfectly well without your adding anything. Second, ordinary people. Bankei spoke everyday Japanese, not the scholar's Chinese of the sutras. Records of his talks show farmers, townspeople, women and men, monks and lay people coming to listen. He mostly skipped the old koan stories and talked about their actual lives: anger, worry, sleepiness, the neighbors. Third, how the unborn gets lost. Nobody is born angry. Something happens, you want your own way, and you turn the unborn mind into a fighting mind, which Bankei calls trading the Buddha-mind for something smaller. Don't fight the anger with more effort, he says. Just don't make it. Fourth, trust. Bankei was wary of teachers who told students to strain and grind for awakening. His advice is gentle: you already have it, so stop swapping it for something else. On an ordinary day, the unborn sounds like this: the kettle clicks off, and you just hear it. Someone cuts in line, and for one beat, before the story starts, there's only seeing.
screen: `THE BUDDHA-MIND IS UNBORN.` · `PLAIN WORDS FOR ORDINARY PEOPLE.` · `NOBODY IS BORN ANGRY.` · `YOU ALREADY HAVE IT.` · then, large: `STAY UNBORN.`

segments.voice: Sit however is comfortable and notice that seeing is already happening without your effort, and so is feeling: the seat, the air, the breath. When a thought starts building something, a plan, a complaint, a worry, notice the building and don't add the next brick. Come back to what's already working fine on its own; there's nothing to earn here.
The unborn. Bankei's word for the Buddha-mind everyone already has, never produced, so it never falls apart. Today's word.
Your line: the kettle clicks off. What's unborn needs no building. That's day one thousand three.

1004.title: The old pond
1004.hook: Basho's poem of a frog jumping into an old pond: a haiku as a moment of attention
1004.howItsDone: People in Japan and around the world write haiku as a way of paying attention, and some Zen communities and poetry groups hold walks where each person writes a short poem about something seen or heard on the way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bankei and the unborn, the mind nobody has to build. Your line: the kettle clicks off.

Furuike ya, kawazu tobikomu, mizu no oto. That's the whole poem, in Japanese. Said slowly, it barely fills a breath. In plain English: the old pond. A frog jumps in. The sound of water. No moral. No feeling announced. No sunset, no heartbreak. A pond, a frog, a splash. It was written by Matsuo Basho, a Japanese poet who walked the roads with very little and wrote as he went.
screen: `FURUIKE YA.` → `A POND, A FROG, A SPLASH.` → `MATSUO BASHO.`

segments.voice: Basho wasn't a monastery teacher, but tradition says he practiced Zen with a priest, and his poems are often read alongside Zen. Here's why. First, the stillness. Furuike, the old pond. Not lively, not pretty. Old. Still. A quiet so deep it has gone a little mossy. The little word ya after it is a pause, like a held breath: the old pond, and. Second, the event. Kawazu tobikomu, a frog jumps in. Not a heron or a dragon: an ordinary creature at the edge of a pond breaks the stillness. Third, the sound. Mizu no oto, the sound of water. The poem doesn't say the frog is beautiful, or that the speaker felt peace. It stops at the sound and lets the sound be the whole thing. Then, implied, the quiet comes back, a different quiet, because now you heard it break. Readers take this poem more than one way. Some hear impermanence: the splash, and gone. Some hear stillness and movement as one thing, the way Dogen spoke of being-time. Some hear a man paying attention so completely that nothing extra gets in. That last reading points at what a haiku can do: be less a poem about a moment than a moment, set down so cleanly that someone else can step into it, long after, and hear the water.
screen: `THE OLD POND: STILLNESS.` · `A FROG JUMPS IN.` · `THE SOUND OF WATER, AND IT STOPS.` · `A MOMENT, NOT A POEM ABOUT ONE.` · then, large: `MIZU NO OTO.`

segments.voice: Let the breath slow, then look and listen for one small thing really happening right now: a car door, a cup on the table, light on a wall. Find the still thing, the moving thing and the sound or detail that lands, and set them in three short lines in your head, no feelings announced, the way Basho let the frog be a frog. Say them silently once, then let them go and keep listening.
Basho. The Japanese poet whose haiku of the old pond, a frog, and a splash became a model of pure attention. Today's word.
Your line: the sound of water. A splash, and then the quiet again. See you tomorrow.

1005.title: "Is that so?"
1005.hook: the story of Hakuin, falsely blamed for a baby, who says "is that so?" and cares for the child
1005.howItsDone: Zen teachers and Buddhist writers retell the Is that so? story as a teaching on equanimity, and Buddhist teachers present praise and blame alike as passing conditions, an old theme in the Buddha's teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Basho's old pond: a frog jumps in, the sound of water. Your line: the sound of water.

Angry parents are pounding on a temple door. Their unmarried daughter is pregnant, and when they pressed her to name the father, she named the respected Zen master of the village temple. The whole neighborhood has heard. The parents shout their accusation in his face. The master listens, and says three words: Is that so? No denial. No speech. The story is told about Hakuin, a Japanese Zen teacher.
screen: `ANGRY PARENTS AT THE DOOR.` → `THEY BLAME THE MASTER.` → `IS THAT SO?`

segments.voice: It's a story people tell about Hakuin, and nobody can say whether it happened as told. But it has traveled because it shows something clearly. When the baby is born, the family brings the infant to Hakuin and leaves the child with him: you did this, so you raise it. His reputation is gone. People stop coming to hear him. He says, Is that so? And he takes the baby. He begs milk from neighbors and whatever else the child needs, and looks after the little one with care. Time passes. Then the young mother can't bear it anymore and tells her parents the truth: the real father is a young man who works in the fish market. The parents rush back to the temple, ashamed, apologize over and over, and ask for the child back. Hakuin hands the baby over, and says: Is that so? Look at what the three words are doing. The first time, they aren't agreement, and they aren't a lie. They're a refusal to fight over his own name while a baby needs looking after. The second time, they aren't triumph. Praise and blame come and go, and he treats them the same, like weather. Through all of it, the one thing that doesn't change is the care. The story isn't asking anyone to accept every false charge in silence. Some readers hear it as a story about ego, how little Hakuin needed to be seen as right. Others hear it about attention: whatever people said, he kept his eyes on the child.
screen: `A STORY PEOPLE TELL.` · `HE TAKES THE BABY, AND CARES.` · `THE TRUTH COMES OUT.` · `PRAISE AND BLAME, LIKE WEATHER.` · then, large: `IS THAT SO?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a small criticism you've heard lately, fair or unfair, not the worst one, and notice what rises in the body: heat, a tight jaw, a speech getting ready. Let it be there, then silently try Hakuin's words, is that so, and breathe in the space they open before any reply. You can still answer later, and correct the record if you need to.
Hakuin. The Zen teacher the story gives three words, is that so, for blame and praise alike, while he keeps caring for the child. Today's word.
Your line: blame and praise, like weather. The care stays the same. Day one thousand five, done.

1006.title: Hakuin's cure
1006.hook: Hakuin's "Zen sickness" and the butter-ball meditation he learned from a hermit
1006.howItsDone: Some Zen teachers pass on Hakuin's soft-butter method and his practice of settling attention in the lower belly, especially for students who are tense or overstraining, and people read his account in Idle Talk on a Night Boat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hakuin and the baby, and three words for blame and praise alike. Your line: blame and praise, like weather.

Hakuin, the same Zen teacher from yesterday's story, wrote about a time when practice made him sick. As a young monk he threw himself at it, sitting, straining, pushing day and night. Then, in his own telling, his body turned on him. His head burned, his legs felt like ice, his ears rang, he was anxious and couldn't rest, and doctors couldn't help. He called it Zen sickness. So he went looking for a hermit in the mountains.
screen: `STRAINING DAY AND NIGHT.` → `ZEN SICKNESS.` → `A HERMIT IN THE MOUNTAINS.`

segments.voice: The account comes from a short work of Hakuin's, often called Idle Talk on a Night Boat. First, the hermit. Hakuin says he climbed into the hills near Kyoto to find a recluse named Hakuyu, who lived in a cave. Hakuyu told him the trouble wasn't too little practice. He'd pushed all his energy up into his head, and it needed to come down. Second, settling low. Hakuyu taught him to bring attention and breath down into the lower belly, below the navel, and rest it there, especially at night, lying down. Third, the butter, the image at the center of it. Imagine a lump of soft, fragrant butter resting on the crown of your head. Slowly it warms and melts, trickling down over the head, face and shoulders, through the chest and belly, down the back and legs to the soles of the feet, soothing everything it touches. Fourth, the result. In Hakuin's telling he practiced this patiently, recovered over time, and went on to teach it to his own students. Readers differ about the story. Some take the hermit at face value; others think Hakuin shaped the account to make a teaching memorable. Either way, his point is plain: strain for awakening with only your head, and the body pays. Bring the warmth back down. One honest note: this is a meditation, not a medical treatment. Hakuin's lesson is about balance in practice.
screen: `HAKUYU, THE HERMIT.` · `BRING IT DOWN TO THE BELLY.` · `THE BUTTER MELTS, HEAD TO FEET.` · `BALANCE, NOT STRAIN.` · then, large: `THE BUTTER MELTS.`

segments.voice: Sit or lie down comfortably, let the breath settle low in the belly, and picture something soft and warm resting on the top of your head: butter, as Hakuyu said, or warm honey, or sunlight, whatever feels kind. Let it slowly melt over the forehead and jaw, the shoulders, chest and belly, down the legs to the feet, taking its time wherever it meets tightness. Then rest in the warmth that's left.
Hakuin's cure. The soft-butter meditation he says he learned from the hermit Hakuyu, bringing warmth and attention down from the head to the feet. Today's word.
Your line: the butter melts. Warmth, brought back down from the head. Day one thousand six.

1007.title: Ryokan and the thief
1007.hook: the poet-monk wishes he could give the thief the moon in his window
1007.carry: I wish I could give the moon
1007.howItsDone: Ryokan's poems and the stories told about him are read in Zen communities and beyond as pictures of a simple, generous life, and Buddhist teaching names giving, dana, as a practice to cultivate.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hakuin's cure: soft butter on the crown of the head, melting down through the body. Your line was the butter melts.

A small hut on a hillside in Japan belongs to an old monk who owns almost nothing. One night a thief slips in, searches every corner, and finds nothing worth taking. Then the monk comes home and catches him. The thief freezes. The monk, the story goes, isn't angry. He's sorry. You came all this way, he says, and there's nothing here for you. So he takes off his own clothes and hands them over. The thief grabs them and runs into the dark. The monk sits down in his empty doorway and looks up at the moon.
screen: `A THIEF IN AN EMPTY HUT.` → `THE MONK GIVES HIM HIS CLOTHES.` → `THE MOON OVERHEAD.`

segments.voice: It's a story people tell about Ryokan, a Zen monk and poet who lived simply, begging for his food in nearby villages. Tradition remembers him in a hut with a begging bowl, not at the head of a temple, and the thief story fits everything else people remember about him. First, the gift. Ryokan doesn't defend what little he has, and he doesn't lecture. He sees a man who came looking for something and is about to leave with nothing, and that seems to bother him more than the loss. His clothes are the only thing worth giving, so he gives them. Buddhist teaching calls giving dana, and treats it as a practice, not only a kindness: something you do on purpose, again and again, until the hand opens more easily. Second, the moon. After the thief is gone, tradition says, Ryokan wrote a very short poem. In plain English it runs something like: the thief left it behind, the moon in my window. He wished, the story goes, that he could have given the man the moon too. In the poem, the one thing worth having couldn't be carried off. Third, an ordinary day. A thief may never come to your door, but small takings do: a seat, a parking space, the credit for an idea. Ryokan's story doesn't ask how to get it back. It asks what's still in the window that nobody could take, and whether you could give a little more than was taken.
screen: `A STORY TOLD ABOUT RYOKAN.` · `HE GIVES THE THIEF HIS CLOTHES.` · `THE MOON LEFT IN THE WINDOW.` · `WHAT NOBODY COULD TAKE.`

segments.voice: Look around at what's near you and choose one thing you could give away, a book, a jacket, an hour of your time, a kind word you've been holding back, and, if you like, who it's for. Notice the small tug of wanting to keep it, and breathe with it without fighting. Then let your eyes rest on something open, a window, the sky, a light, something nobody can take from you.
Ryokan. The poet-monk who gave a thief his clothes and wished he could give him the moon as well. Today's word.
Your line: I wish I could give the moon. Some things can't be carried off. See you tomorrow.

1008.title: Ryokan plays
1008.hook: Ryokan plays hide and seek with village children till after dark
1008.howItsDone: Ryokan's poems about children and play are read in Zen communities and in Japanese schools and homes, and his story is told as a picture of practice that includes simple joy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ryokan and the thief: the monk who gave away his clothes and kept the moon. Your line was I wish I could give the moon.
screen: `I WISH I COULD GIVE THE MOON.`

segments.voice: Late afternoon in a village. Children run up to an old monk with a begging bowl and shout his name, not for a blessing, but to ask him to play. He sets the bowl down. They play ball, then hide and seek, and when it's his turn to hide he crawls into a pile of straw in a field and goes perfectly still. The children search. It gets dark. They go home for supper and forget all about him. The next morning, the story goes, a farmer comes to move the straw and finds the monk still there. Shh, the monk whispers. The children will find me.
screen: `THE CHILDREN WANT TO PLAY.` → `HE HIDES IN THE STRAW.` → `SHH. THEY'LL FIND ME.`

segments.voice: Like the thief story, this is a story people tell about Ryokan. Versions differ on where he hid; the monk stays the same. First, play as practice. Ryokan's poems, as they've come down to us, keep returning to children, to a ball, to a spring day that ends too soon. Tradition says he carried a cloth handball in his sleeve. For him, playing doesn't seem to have been time stolen from practice. It was a place practice showed up: full attention, no score worth keeping, no reputation to protect. Second, still hiding. Why stay all night? Some readers hear a holy fool, too simple to notice the game was over. Others hear faithfulness: he gave his word to the game, and kept it. Others hear complete absorption, so present to hiding that nobody was left inside to give up. The story doesn't choose for you. Third, the week behind us, a week of teachers from Japan. Bassui asked who is hearing. Bankei pointed to the unborn mind, already here. Basho heard the sound of water when a frog jumped into an old pond. Hakuin, blamed for a baby that wasn't his, said is that so, and taught the butter that melts. Ryokan gave away his clothes and kept the moon. And today he's in the straw, still hiding, waiting for the children to come back.
screen: `VERSIONS DIFFER ON WHERE HE HID.` · `PLAY AS A PLACE FOR PRACTICE.` · `WHY STAY ALL NIGHT?` · `A WEEK OF TEACHERS FROM JAPAN.`

segments.voice: Pick something small and playful, tapping a rhythm on your knee, balancing a pen on one finger, humming a tune, tossing a balled-up sock from hand to hand, and do it with your whole attention, the way a child does when nothing else exists. When your mind starts grading how silly this is, notice that, and go back to playing.
Ryokan plays. The monk who hid in the straw for the children's game and was still hiding at dawn. Today's word.
Your line: still hiding. For Ryokan, play could be practice, too. Day one thousand eight, done.
